subject: The World Around Us
title: Ravi and Priya Protect Our Planet
hook: Two friends learn how Earth supports all life and explore ways to protect it for future generations.

slides.title: Earth - Our Shared Home
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya visit an environmental center with Eco Uncle to learn about protecting our planet.

image.alt: Earth - Our Shared Home — Earth - Our Shared Home

slides.title: One Planet, Many Lives
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle begins: 'Earth is our shared home. It sustains 8 billion humans and millions of animal and plant species. Today, we learn how to care for it.'

slides.title: Earth's Structure and Resources
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle shows a globe with layers: 'Earth has a solid crust, liquid interior, and atmosphere. Each provides resources we need.'

points.text: The crust is Earth's solid outer layer with soil, minerals, and rocks.
Beneath the crust is the mantle and core, generating Earth's heat.
Oceans cover 71% of Earth; land covers 29%.
The atmosphere (air) protects us from harmful sun rays and keeps us warm.
Soil, water, forests, minerals, and fossil fuels are Earth's natural resources.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth is layered like an onion, with a crust, mantle, and core, surrounded by an atmosphere that protects all life.

slides.title: Priya's Discovery at the Aquarium
slides.storyContext: Priya watches fish swimming and says, 'Every creature depends on this water. If the ocean gets polluted, these animals die.' Eco Uncle nods: 'That's why we must protect every corner of Earth.'

points.text: Water covers most of Earth and is home to millions of species.
Oceans regulate climate and produce oxygen.

slides.title: Biodiversity - The Web of Life
slides.storyContext: Priya looks at pictures of rainforests, coral reefs, and grasslands. 'So many different creatures! They're all connected,' she says.

points.text: Biodiversity means the variety of all living organisms and ecosystems on Earth.
Over 8 million species of animals, plants, fungi, and microbes exist.
Each species plays a role: plants produce oxygen, pollinators spread seeds, predators control pests.
Ecosystems are communities of organisms and their environment, interdependent.
Rainforests, grasslands, deserts, oceans, and wetlands each have unique biodiversity.
Loss of one species can affect the whole ecosystem.

slides.inSimpleWords: Biodiversity is the incredible variety of life—millions of species—all connected in webs where each plays an important role.

slides.title: Food Chains: Who Eats What?
slides.storyContext: Ravi draws a food chain: 'Grass is eaten by rabbits, and rabbits are eaten by eagles. If grass dies, rabbits starve, and eagles starve too!'

example.problem: In a grassland ecosystem, if all the flowers die, what happens to the bees and birds that eat the flowers?
example.solution: Bees and birds lose their food source and must move elsewhere or starve. The ecosystem breaks down.

slides.title: Environmental Problems
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle shows photos of pollution, deforestation, and climate change. 'These problems threaten our home,' he says gravely.

points.label: Air Pollution
points.text: Smoke from factories, vehicles, and burning waste makes air toxic, causing health problems.

points.label: Water Pollution
points.text: Chemicals, plastic waste, and sewage contaminate rivers and oceans, harming aquatic life.

points.label: Soil Pollution
points.text: Pesticides and industrial waste make soil unhealthy, reducing crop yield.

points.label: Deforestation
points.text: Cutting forests for timber and farmland destroys habitats and reduces oxygen production.

points.label: Climate Change
points.text: Burning fossil fuels releases CO₂, trapping heat and warming Earth, causing extreme weather.

points.label: Plastic Waste
points.text: Plastic lasts hundreds of years, choking oceans and harming wildlife.

slides.inSimpleWords: Our planet faces serious problems: air, water, and soil pollution; loss of forests; rising temperatures; and mountains of plastic waste.

slides.title: Ravi Sees Pollution in His City
slides.storyContext: Ravi looks at the smoggy sky over the city and coughs. 'Why is the air so bad?' he asks. Eco Uncle explains: 'Car exhaust, factory smoke, and burning waste create smog. It makes us sick and harms plants too.'

points.text: Smog reduces visibility and harms lungs.
Polluted air weakens trees and crops.

slides.title: Conservation and Sustainable Living
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle smiles: 'But we can fix these problems! It starts with us making smart choices.'

points.label: Reduce
points.text: Use less. Buy only what you need. Avoid single-use plastics.

points.label: Reuse
points.text: Use things again: old clothes as rags, glass jars as containers, paper bags instead of plastic.

points.label: Recycle
points.text: Separate waste: paper, plastic, metal, glass. Factories turn recycled materials into new products.

points.label: Plant Trees
points.text: Trees clean air, provide shade, and give homes to animals.

points.label: Save Water
points.text: Turn off taps, take short showers, fix leaks, use rainwater harvesting.

points.label: Save Energy
points.text: Use LED bulbs, turn off lights, avoid air conditioning when possible.

slides.inSimpleWords: We can protect Earth by reducing waste, reusing items, recycling, planting trees, and saving water and energy.

slides.title: Priya's Zero-Waste Lunch Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya brings lunch in a steel container and glass bottle instead of plastic bags. 'No trash!' she announces proudly. Ravi tries it too and saves 5 plastic bags per week.

example.problem: If one child reduces plastic waste by 5 bags per week, and there are 100 children in a school doing this, how many plastic bags are saved per week? Per year?
example.solution: Per week: 100 × 5 = 500 bags. Per year: 500 × 52 = 26,000 bags saved! One school prevents 26,000 bags from polluting our oceans.

slides.title: Renewable Energy - Clean Power
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle shows solar panels on the roof. 'Energy from the sun, wind, and water are clean and endless.'

points.label: Solar Energy
points.text: Panels convert sunlight into electricity. No pollution, lasts millions of years.

points.label: Wind Energy
points.text: Wind turbines use wind to generate electricity. Common in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat.

points.label: Hydroelectric Energy
points.text: Dams use flowing water to produce electricity without burning fossil fuels.

points.label: Biogas
points.text: Farm waste and cow dung are converted to cooking gas, reducing waste.
Renewable energy replaces coal, oil, and natural gas, stopping greenhouse gas emissions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Renewable energy from the sun, wind, and water powers homes without pollution and lasts forever.

image.alt: Renewable Energy - Clean Power — Earth - Our Shared Home

slides.title: Visit to a Solar Village
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya visit a village powered entirely by solar energy. Every house has panels, and the village has no pollution. 'This is the future!' says Priya excitedly.

points.text: Solar villages prove renewable energy works at scale.
Communities can be fully powered by clean energy.

slides.title: Comparing Energy Sources
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle compares: 'Coal plants produce electricity but emit 1 ton of CO₂ per megawatt. Solar produces zero emissions.'

example.problem: If a coal plant produces 1,000 tons of CO₂ per day and a solar plant produces 0 tons, how much CO₂ does coal produce in a year compared to solar?
example.solution: Coal: 1,000 × 365 = 365,000 tons CO₂ per year. Solar: 0 tons. Coal produces 365,000 more tons of harmful emissions annually.

slides.title: Global Cooperation for Earth
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks: 'Can one country fix Earth's problems alone?' Eco Uncle shakes his head: 'No, the whole world must work together.'

points.text: The United Nations brings countries together to protect the environment.
Paris Climate Agreement: Nations pledged to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Protected areas and national parks preserve biodiversity.
International laws ban harmful chemicals and regulate whaling and poaching.
NGOs (non-governmental organizations) work globally on environmental issues.
Young activists push governments to act faster on climate change.

slides.inSimpleWords: Countries, organizations, and people worldwide must work together to protect oceans, forests, atmosphere, and wildlife.

image.alt: Global Cooperation for Earth — Earth - Our Shared Home

slides.title: India's Role in Climate Action
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle shares: 'India has committed to planting 70 billion trees and shifting to 50% renewable energy by 2030. Every Indian can help!'

points.text: India is a global leader in renewable energy expansion.
Youth movements in India push for stronger climate policies.

slides.title: Carbon Footprint Calculation
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle teaches them: 'Every activity releases carbon dioxide. This is your carbon footprint.'

example.problem: Ravi's family activities per day: car drive = 2 kg CO₂, electricity use = 1.5 kg CO₂, food = 1 kg CO₂, waste = 0.5 kg CO₂. What is their daily carbon footprint? Weekly?
example.solution: Daily: 2 + 1.5 + 1 + 0.5 = 5 kg CO₂. Weekly: 5 × 7 = 35 kg CO₂. They can reduce by using public transport, saving electricity, eating less meat, and reducing waste.

slides.title: Personal Environmental Footprint
slides.storyContext: Priya calculates her family's footprint and realizes even small changes add up: 'If I walk instead of taking a car 3 times a week, I save 6 kg of CO₂!'

points.label: Food Footprint
points.text: Meat production uses more water and land than vegetables.

points.label: Transport Footprint
points.text: Cars emit CO₂; public transport and walking are cleaner.

points.label: Energy Footprint
points.text: Electricity from coal is dirtier than solar or wind.

points.label: Waste Footprint
points.text: Recycling reduces the energy needed to make new products.

slides.inSimpleWords: Your carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gases your activities produce. Small changes in daily habits reduce it significantly.

slides.title: Ravi and Priya's School Project Proposal
slides.storyContext: At school, Ravi and Priya present their eco-project idea to the principal: a school garden using compost, rainwater harvesting, and solar lights to power everything.

points.text: Students can lead environmental projects at school.
Small school projects inspire whole communities.

slides.title: Design Your Eco-Project
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya are inspired: 'What can we do at home or school to help Earth?'

example.problem: Design a project to reduce waste, save water, or plant trees at your home or school. What will you do? How many people will participate? What is your goal?
example.solution: Example: Start a composting program at school. Collect vegetable waste from the cafeteria, compost it in the garden for 3 months, and use the compost to grow vegetables. Goal: reduce waste by 50% and grow 20 kg of organic vegetables for the school kitchen.

slides.title: Circular Economy: Waste to Treasure
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle explains: 'In a circular economy, waste from one process becomes input for another. Nothing is truly wasted.'

points.label: Old Clothes
points.text: Donated clothes are reused; worn ones become rags or insulation.

points.label: Plastic Waste
points.text: Recycled plastic becomes benches, bags, or construction materials.

points.label: Food Waste
points.text: Composted food scraps grow new vegetables and plants.

points.label: Paper
points.text: Shredded paper becomes packaging or cardboard.

slides.inSimpleWords: A circular economy recycles waste into new useful products, protecting resources and reducing pollution.

slides.title: From Plastic Bottles to Park Benches
slides.storyContext: Priya visits a recycling center and sees plastic bottles being shredded and molded into park benches. '1,000 bottles make one bench!' says the worker.

example.problem: If each park bench requires 1,000 plastic bottles and a park has 20 benches, how many bottles were recycled? If an average person uses 52 bottles per year, how many people's annual waste makes these benches?
example.solution: Bottles for benches: 20 × 1,000 = 20,000 bottles. People's annual waste: 20,000 ÷ 52 ≈ 385 people's yearly bottles used in just one park.

slides.title: Protecting Earth's Ecosystems
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle highlights critical ecosystems: 'Rainforests, coral reefs, and wetlands are Earth's lungs. We must protect them completely.'

points.label: Rainforests
points.text: Produce 20% of Earth's oxygen; home to 50% of all species; regulate rainfall.

points.label: Coral Reefs
points.text: Support 25% of ocean life; protect coastlines from storms; provide food and medicine.

points.label: Wetlands
points.text: Filter water; prevent floods; provide homes for birds and fish.

points.label: Forests
points.text: Store carbon, prevent erosion, and sustain millions of lives.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth's critical ecosystems like rainforests, reefs, and wetlands must be protected because they sustain all life.

slides.title: Visiting a Protected Forest Reserve
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya trek through a protected rainforest. They spot rare birds, jaguars, and undiscovered plants. 'This is why we must protect forests!' says Priya in wonder.

points.text: Protected areas preserve biodiversity and wildlife habitats.
Ecotourism provides income for local communities to conserve forests.

slides.title: Mangrove Forests and Coastal Protection
slides.storyContext: Eco Uncle explains: 'Mangroves are special trees that grow in water. They protect coastlines from storms and provide homes for fish, crabs, and birds.'

example.problem: A coastal area with 100 hectares of mangrove forest is protected. Each hectare provides habitat for 500 species. If mangroves are cut down, how many species lose their homes?
example.solution: Total species: 100 × 500 = 50,000 species would lose homes if all mangroves are destroyed. This is why protection is critical.

slides.title: The Friends Make a Promise
slides.storyContext: As the day ends, Ravi and Priya make a promise to Eco Uncle: 'We will use less, plant trees, save water and energy, and inspire others to protect Earth.'

points.text: Individual actions create collective change.
Young people can be environmental leaders.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: As they leave the environmental center, Ravi and Priya feel empowered and hopeful.

points.text: Earth is our shared home with incredible biodiversity and natural resources.
Environmental problems—pollution, deforestation, climate change—threaten all life.
The 3 R's (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle) and conservation actions can protect Earth.
Renewable energy from sun, wind, and water replaces dirty fossil fuels.
Global cooperation is essential: countries, organizations, and individuals must work together.
Young people like Ravi and Priya are the future guardians of Earth.
Small actions by millions of people can create big, positive change.
A circular economy reduces waste and protects Earth's limited resources.
Protecting critical ecosystems like rainforests and coral reefs sustains all life on Earth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth is our only home, and protecting it is everyone's responsibility. By reducing waste, saving resources, and acting together, we can create a healthy planet for future generations.

subject: Mathematics
title: Anaya and Ravi's Sweet Cake Adventure
hook: Two friends divide a birthday cake and discover the magic of fractions.

slides.title: Fractions: Parts of a Whole
slides.storyContext: Anaya and Ravi discover the magic of fractions through cakes, ribbons, and everyday objects.

image.alt: Fractions: Parts of a Whole — Fractions

slides.title: The Birthday Cake Puzzle
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother baked a big round cake. She asked Anaya and Ravi to divide it fairly among their 4 friends. Anaya cut the cake into 4 equal pieces.

points.label: Setup
points.text: One whole cake divided into 4 equal parts

slides.inSimpleWords: One cake cut into 4 equal pieces makes fractions.

slides.title: Understanding Numerator and Denominator
slides.storyContext: Ravi pointed at one slice. 'That's 1 out of 4 pieces,' he said. Anaya wrote: 1/4.

points.label: Numerator
points.text: The number on top (1) = how many pieces we take

points.label: Denominator
points.text: The number below (4) = total equal pieces

points.label: Fraction
points.text: 1/4 means one part out of four

points.label: Read It
points.text: 1/4 is read as 'one-fourth' or 'one-quarter'

slides.inSimpleWords: Top number = pieces taken. Bottom number = total pieces.

slides.title: Sharing Among Friends
slides.storyContext: When Ravi takes 1 slice, he has 1/4 of the cake. When Anaya takes 2 slices, she has 2/4. Their friend Tina takes 1 slice, and Ravi's brother takes the last slice.

points.text: 4/4 means all four pieces, which is the complete cake.

slides.title: Fractions as Division
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother says: 'Cutting the cake into equal parts is like dividing. 1/4 means divide 1 cake by 4 people.'

points.label: Division
points.text: A fraction is a way to show division: a ÷ b = a/b

points.label: One Cake, 4 People
points.text: 1 ÷ 4 = 1/4 (each person gets one-fourth)

points.label: One Pizza, 8 Slices
points.text: 1 ÷ 8 = 1/8 (each slice is one-eighth)

points.label: Fair Share
points.text: Fractions help divide things equally among people.

slides.inSimpleWords: A fraction shows how to divide one thing into equal parts and share them fairly.

slides.title: Working with Fractions
slides.storyContext: Anaya took 2 slices for herself and Ravi. That was 2/4 of the cake.

example.problem: If Anaya eats 2 slices out of 4, what fraction is that?
example.solution: 2 slices taken ÷ 4 total slices = 2/4 (which simplifies to 1/2)

points.label: Remember
points.text: Multiple parts of the same fraction add together

slides.inSimpleWords: Two slices out of four is 2/4 or half the cake.

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Ravi's mother cut another identical cake into 8 pieces. Ravi took 4 slices from this cake. 'Look, Anaya! I have the same amount as you!' he said.

points.label: Same Amount
points.text: 2/4 from first cake = 4/8 from second cake

points.label: Equivalent
points.text: Different fractions, same value

points.label: Multiply
points.text: 2/4 × 2/2 = 4/8 (multiply top and bottom by same number)

points.label: Divide
points.text: 4/8 ÷ 2/2 = 2/4 (divide top and bottom by same number)

slides.inSimpleWords: Half a cake = 2/4 = 4/8. Different numbers, same part.

slides.title: The Ribbon Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya has a ribbon and cuts it into 3 equal pieces. She gives Ravi 1 piece (1/3) and keeps 2 pieces for herself (2/3). 'Look, I have twice as much as you!' laughs Anaya.

points.text: 1/3 + 2/3 = 3/3 = 1 whole ribbon
2/3 is twice as much as 1/3

slides.title: Comparing Fractions
slides.storyContext: At the party, Anaya's friend got 1/2 of a chocolate bar, and another friend got 2/4 of an identical bar. 'They're the same!' said Ravi.

example.solution: 1/2 = 2/4. They are equal; neither is bigger.

points.label: Tip
points.text: Draw or fold paper to see equivalent fractions

slides.inSimpleWords: 1/2 and 2/4 are the same amount, just different names.

slides.title: Comparing Different Fractions
slides.storyContext: Ravi compares his chocolate bar piece (1/3) with Anaya's (1/4). 'Mine is bigger because I only divided mine into 3 pieces, but you divided yours into 4!'

points.label: Same Numerator
points.text: 1/3 > 1/4 (fewer pieces = bigger pieces)

points.label: Same Denominator
points.text: 2/4 > 1/4 (more pieces taken = more chocolate)

points.label: Finding Common Denominator
points.text: Convert 1/2 and 1/3 to 3/6 and 2/6 to compare easily.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare fractions by finding common denominators or by visualizing pieces of the same whole.

slides.title: Your Fraction Challenge
slides.storyContext: Anaya has a ribbon 1 meter long. She cuts it into 5 equal pieces for her hair clips. Ravi asks: 'What fraction is each piece?'

points.label: Think
points.text: If 1 ribbon is cut into 5 equal pieces, each piece is __/5

slides.inSimpleWords: One ribbon, five equal pieces: each piece is 1/5.

slides.title: Fractions in Daily Life
slides.storyContext: Anaya realized fractions are everywhere: half a glass of milk, one-third of the journey completed, two-quarter hours at school.

points.label: Milk
points.text: 1/2 cup of milk

points.label: Time
points.text: 1/3 of the day

points.label: Distance
points.text: 2/4 of the road

points.label: Recipes
points.text: 1/4 cup flour, 1/2 cup sugar

points.label: Money
points.text: 1/2 rupee, 1/4 of your pocket money

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions help us describe parts of things in real life.

slides.title: Helping Anaya's Mother Bake
slides.storyContext: Anaya's mother bakes a cake using the recipe: 1/2 cup butter, 1/4 cup milk, 3/4 cup flour. Anaya realizes measuring uses fractions constantly!

points.text: Baking requires precise fraction measurements.
Too much or too little changes the whole cake.

slides.title: Adding Simple Fractions
slides.storyContext: Ravi ate 1/4 of a pizza. Anaya ate 2/4 of the same pizza. Together, how much did they eat?

points.label: Rule
points.text: Same denominator? Add top numbers only.

slides.inSimpleWords: 1/4 plus 2/4 equals 3/4 of the pizza.

slides.title: Subtracting Fractions
slides.storyContext: Anaya had 3/4 of a chocolate bar. She gave Ravi 1/4. How much does she have left? 3/4 - 1/4 = 2/4.

points.label: Same Denominator
points.text: Subtract numerators, keep denominator same

points.label: Check
points.text: Make sure you have enough: can't subtract 3/4 from 1/4

slides.inSimpleWords: To subtract fractions with same denominator, subtract top numbers and keep the bottom number.

slides.title: Fractions with Different Denominators
slides.storyContext: Ravi ate 1/2 of a sandwich and Anaya ate 1/4 of an identical sandwich. How much did they eat together? 1/2 + 1/4 = ?

slides.title: Proper and Improper Fractions
slides.storyContext: Anaya's bakery sold cakes in pieces. If someone bought 5 pieces when each whole cake had 4 pieces, that's 5/4 (more than one whole cake!).

points.label: Proper Fraction
points.text: Numerator < Denominator (less than 1 whole)

points.label: Improper Fraction
points.text: Numerator ≥ Denominator (more than or equal to 1 whole)

points.label: Mixed Number
points.text: 5/4 = 1 and 1/4 (one whole plus one-quarter)

slides.inSimpleWords: 5/4 is bigger than one whole cake piece.

slides.title: Ravi and Anaya's Pizza Party Puzzle
slides.storyContext: They order 2 pizzas cut into 8 slices each (16 slices total). They eat 20 slices. That's 20/16 or 1 and 4/16 pizzas! They ate more than 1 whole pizza.

points.text: 20/16 is an improper fraction.
20/16 = 1 4/16 = 1 1/4 as a mixed number.

slides.title: Multiplying a Fraction by a Whole Number
slides.storyContext: Anaya has 1/4 of a chocolate bar. Ravi gives her 3 more identical bars. How much chocolate does she have now? 3 × 1/4 = 3/4.

example.problem: If Anaya has 1/4 of a bar and gets 3 more bars (4/4 each), how much does she have in total? 1/4 + 4/4 + 4/4 + 4/4 = ?

slides.title: Simplifying (Reducing) Fractions
slides.storyContext: Ravi notices: '4/8 and 1/2 are the same! We can simplify 4/8 by dividing both top and bottom by 4.'

points.label: Simplify
points.text: Divide numerator and denominator by the same number

points.label: Check
points.text: Stop when you can't divide anymore (lowest terms)

slides.inSimpleWords: Simplify a fraction by dividing top and bottom by the same number until you can't divide anymore.

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Fraction Mastery
slides.storyContext: After practicing fractions everywhere they look—in recipes, ribbons, pizzas, and sandwiches—Anaya and Ravi feel confident. 'Fractions are everywhere!' says Anaya.

points.text: Fractions are essential math tools used daily.
Mastering fractions opens doors to advanced mathematics.

slides.title: Anaya and Ravi's Fraction Lesson
slides.storyContext: The friends learned that fractions are parts of wholes, written with numerator and denominator, and found everywhere from cakes to ribbons to journeys.

points.label: Numerator
points.text: Number of parts we take (top)

points.label: Denominator
points.text: Total equal parts (bottom)

points.label: Equivalent
points.text: Different fractions, same value

points.label: Adding
points.text: Same denominator: add numerators

points.label: Subtracting
points.text: Same denominator: subtract numerators

points.label: Simplify
points.text: Divide top and bottom by the same number

points.label: Real Life
points.text: Fractions describe portions of everything

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions name parts of a whole using two numbers.

image.alt: Anaya and Ravi's Fraction Lesson — Fractions

subject: Mathematics
title: Ravi and Anaya's Compass Adventure
hook: Two friends use a spinning compass to discover how turns create angles.

slides.title: Angles as Turns
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Anaya explore angles by spinning, turning, and measuring all around them.

image.alt: Angles as Turns — Angles as Turns

slides.title: The Spinning Compass Game
slides.storyContext: Ravi found a toy compass on the beach. Anaya asked him to spin it slowly. 'When it completes one full turn, that's a complete angle,' she explained, pointing at how the needle went all the way around.

points.label: Complete Turn
points.text: One full spin = 360 degrees

slides.inSimpleWords: One full spin around is called 360 degrees.

slides.title: What is an Angle?
slides.storyContext: Anaya explains: 'An angle is formed when two lines meet at a point. The angle measures HOW MUCH we turn from one line to the other.'

points.label: Angle
points.text: Formed by two rays sharing an endpoint (vertex)

points.label: Vertex
points.text: The point where two rays meet

points.label: Measure
points.text: Measured in degrees (°)

points.label: Symbol
points.text: We write 45° to mean 45 degrees

slides.inSimpleWords: An angle shows how much you turn from one direction to another.

slides.title: Ravi's Spinning Movements
slides.storyContext: Ravi stands and spins around: 'When I face north and turn to face east, I've turned 90 degrees. When I face south, I've turned 180 degrees!'

points.text: A 90-degree turn is one quarter of a full spin.
A 180-degree turn is half a full spin.

slides.title: Understanding Right Angles
slides.storyContext: Anaya held the compass steady and told Ravi to spin it just one-quarter of the way. 'Stop!' she said. The needle had turned 90 degrees. 'That's a right angle,' Anaya smiled, 'like the corner of our classroom door.'

points.label: Right Angle
points.text: 90 degrees = one quarter turn

points.label: Symbol
points.text: A small square in the corner marks a right angle

points.label: Examples
points.text: Corners of books, doors, windows

points.label: Perpendicular
points.text: Two lines that form a right angle are perpendicular

slides.inSimpleWords: 90 degrees is one-quarter turn, like a door corner.

image.alt: Understanding Right Angles — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Measuring Angles with Turns
slides.storyContext: Ravi turned the compass halfway around. Anaya counted: '180 degrees! That's a straight line, Ravi.' They realized half a turn makes a straight angle.

example.problem: If Ravi spins the compass halfway, how many degrees has he turned?

points.label: Straight Angle
points.text: 180 degrees = half turn

slides.inSimpleWords: Halfway around is 180 degrees, making a straight line.

image.alt: Measuring Angles with Turns — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Acute, Right, and Obtuse Angles
slides.storyContext: Anaya taught Ravi three types of angles using her arms. A small hug (arms close) = acute angle (less than 90°). Arms at a corner = right angle (90°). A big hug (arms wide) = obtuse angle (more than 90° but less than 180°).

points.label: Acute
points.text: Less than 90 degrees (small angle)

points.label: Right
points.text: Exactly 90 degrees (corner)

points.label: Obtuse
points.text: More than 90 but less than 180 degrees (wide)

points.label: Reflex
points.text: More than 180 degrees but less than 360 degrees

slides.inSimpleWords: Three angle types: small, corner, or wide hug.

slides.title: Spotting Angles Everywhere at School
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Anaya walk around their school: the corner of a book (90°), the open lid (60°), the staircase (120°), and the open window (100°).

points.text: Right angles appear in doors, corners, windows.
Acute angles appear in roof peaks and open scissors.
Obtuse angles appear in wide-open doors and fans.

slides.title: Finding Angles in Your Classroom
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Anaya walked around their school. They found a right angle where the wall meets the floor (90°), an acute angle at the roof peak, and an obtuse angle at the open window.

example.problem: The window opens 120 degrees. Is this acute, right, or obtuse?
example.solution: 120° is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it's obtuse.

points.label: Remember
points.text: 90° = right, less = acute, more = obtuse

slides.inSimpleWords: 120 degrees is wider than a corner, so it's obtuse.

image.alt: Finding Angles in Your Classroom — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Protractor: The Angle Measuring Tool
slides.storyContext: Anaya pulled out a protractor. 'This tool measures angles!' she said. She placed it on the compass where the needle pointed and read the number: 45 degrees. Ravi marveled: 'That's exactly one-eighth of a full turn!'

points.label: Protractor
points.text: A semicircle with numbers 0-180

points.label: How to Use
points.text: Center at the angle point, align one ray at 0

points.label: Two Scales
points.text: Inner scale (0-180 left to right) and outer scale (180-0 left to right)

points.label: Read Carefully
points.text: Choose the scale that matches your angle opening

slides.inSimpleWords: A protractor measures angles using its numbered semicircle.

image.alt: Protractor: The Angle Measuring Tool — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Anaya Measures Angles Precisely
slides.storyContext: Anaya uses her protractor to measure the angles of different objects: a pencil tilted at 35°, a door open at 85°, a roof peak at 60°, and a wide-open fan at 140°.

points.text: Different objects have different angle measures.
A protractor gives exact measurements.

slides.title: Estimate the Angle
slides.storyContext: Ravi opened the door slowly and asked Anaya to guess the angle without measuring. The door was open about a quarter way. 'About 90 degrees?' guessed Anaya. Ravi smiled: 'Close! It's actually 85 degrees.'

points.label: Skill
points.text: Estimating helps before you measure

slides.inSimpleWords: Try guessing angles before you measure them.

image.alt: Estimate the Angle — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Clock Angles
slides.storyContext: Anaya noticed the school clock. 'The hour hand and minute hand make angles!' She calculated: at 3 o'clock, the hands make a 90-degree angle. At 6 o'clock, they make 180 degrees.

example.problem: At 3:00, what angle do the clock hands make?
example.solution: Hour hand at 3, minute hand at 12 = 90 degrees (right angle)

points.label: Clock Facts
points.text: Each hour = 30 degrees (360° ÷ 12 hours)

slides.inSimpleWords: Clock hands make angles that change every minute.

slides.title: Angles in Geometry Shapes
slides.storyContext: Ravi draws shapes: a square (four 90° angles), a triangle (three angles that add to 180°), and a pentagon (five angles that add to 540°).

points.label: Triangle
points.text: 3 angles that add up to 180°

points.label: Square/Rectangle
points.text: 4 angles that add up to 360° (four 90° angles)

points.label: Pentagon
points.text: 5 angles that add up to 540°

points.label: Formula
points.text: Sum of angles = (n - 2) × 180°, where n is number of sides

slides.inSimpleWords: Every shape has angles inside it, and the total depends on how many sides it has.

slides.title: Measuring Triangle Angles
slides.storyContext: Anaya draws a triangle and measures its three angles: 60°, 60°, and 60°. 'They add up to 180!' she says. Then she draws another triangle with 90°, 45°, and 45°. 'This one also adds to 180!'

example.problem: A triangle has angles of 70° and 50°. What is the third angle?

slides.title: Angles in Nature and Design
slides.storyContext: Ravi pointed at the river flowing and Anaya at the trees. 'Branches make angles!' said Ravi. 'So do river bends,' added Anaya. They realized angles were everywhere: bird wings, roofs, ladders, and even the way people sit.

points.label: Nature
points.text: Tree branches, bird wings, petals

points.label: Design
points.text: Roofs, stairs, furniture

points.label: Body
points.text: Arms, legs, joints

points.label: Engineering
points.text: Bridges, dams, buildings use specific angles for strength

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles are found in nature, buildings, and our bodies.

image.alt: Angles in Nature and Design — Angles as Turns

slides.title: Discovering Angles in Sports
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Anaya watch a cricket match and notice: the bowler's arm angle, the batsman's swing angle, and the angle at which the ball flies through the air all matter for the sport.

points.text: Sports use angles for accuracy and power.
A good bowling angle and bat angle are crucial for scoring.

slides.title: Angles in Architecture
slides.storyContext: Anaya visits a construction site and sees: a roof peak at 60°, staircase steps at 30°, and door hinges opening at 120°. Each angle is designed for a specific purpose.

example.problem: A roof peak is 45° on one side and 45° on the other. What is the total angle of the roof peak?
example.solution: 45° + 45° = 90°, forming a right angle at the peak where both sides meet.

slides.title: Ravi and Anaya's Angle Mastery
slides.storyContext: After exploring angles in clocks, shapes, nature, sports, and buildings, Ravi and Anaya have discovered that angles are everywhere and essential to understanding the world.

points.text: Angles are fundamental to geometry and real-world applications.
Measuring angles precisely is a critical skill in many fields.

slides.title: Ravi and Anaya's Angle Discovery
slides.storyContext: The friends learned that angles measure turns, come in different sizes (acute, right, obtuse), and are measured in degrees using a protractor. They're everywhere!

points.label: Full Turn
points.text: 360 degrees

points.label: Half Turn
points.text: 180 degrees (straight)

points.label: Quarter Turn
points.text: 90 degrees (right angle)

points.label: Angle Types
points.text: Acute (<90°), Right (=90°), Obtuse (>90°), Reflex (>180°)

points.label: Measurement
points.text: Use a protractor to measure angles precisely

points.label: Shapes
points.text: Triangle angles add to 180°, quadrilateral angles add to 360°

points.label: All Around
points.text: Angles in nature, buildings, clocks, sports, and more

slides.inSimpleWords: Angles measure turns and are found everywhere we look.
